attachment.content:
- deep-research: Deep research harness — fan-out web searches, fetch sources, adversarially verify claims, synthesize a cited report. - When the user wants a deep, multi-source, fact-checked research report on any topic. BEFORE invoking, check if the question is specific enough to research directly — if underspecified (e.g., "what car to buy" without budget/use-case/region), ask 2-3 clarifying questions to narrow scope. Then pass the refined question as args, weaving the answers in.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- verify: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by exercising it end-to-end and observing behavior — drive the affected flow, not just tests or typecheck. Run before committing nontrivial changes; bootstraps this repo's project verify skill if none exists yet. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.
- code-review: Review the current diff for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings). Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo, defaults to 10m) - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- review: Review a GitHub pull request; for your working diff use /code-review
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

input.approach_name: Faithful hopscotch: flat bucket array + per-bucket neighbourhood bitmap + backward hopping (with load-factor growth and a bounded overflow list as the termination guarantee)
module_layout: /output/test15.rs — PACKAGE-ROOT ENTRY (required). Holds only two `#[path]` mod declarations plus `fn main()`, which is a line-by-line transliteration of test15.cpp (argv gate -> stoi -> insert loop -> equal_range -> count -> println!). No table logic here. Verified working today.

/output/Cargo.toml — `[[bin]] name = "test15", path = "test15.rs"`, edition 2021, empty `[dependencies]`. MUST NOT gain a `src/lib.rs` or `src/main.rs` (see risks: that is the one change that breaks the dual build).

/output/src/tsl/mod.rs — the `tsl` namespace facade. `pub mod hash; pub mod hopscotch_hash; pub mod hopscotch_map;` (plain sibling resolution — no further `#[path]` needed) plus `pub use` re-exports so test15.rs can say `tsl::HopscotchMap`. Carries `#![allow(dead_code, unused_imports)]` because the bin exercises only a fraction of the API.

/output/src/tsl/hash.rs — hashers standing in for `std::hash<int>`. `IdentityHasher`/`BuildIdentityHasher` (libstdc++ identity semantics for primitives, FNV-1a fallback for bytes) and `MixingHasher`/`BuildMixingHasher` (Fibonacci + xorshift finish) for key sets with poor low-bit entropy. Exists; needs the clobbering fix in risks.

Flat `Vec<Bucket<K,V>>` with trailing anti-wrap slack, neighbourhood bitmaps, linear probe, backward hop, load-factor rehash, overflow list, and flat `Pos` iteration primitives (`first_pos`/`pos_after`/`entry_at`/`end_pos`). Exists at ~773 lines; needs two fixes in risks.

This is the only file the port's main() touches.

input.core_data_structures:
BUCKET (the whole trick):

    pub struct Bucket<K, V> {
        neighbourhood: u32,          // bit d set => slot (self+d) holds an entry homed HERE
        entry: Option<(K, V)>,       // in-place slot, no per-entry heap allocation
    }

Measured `size_of::<Bucket<i32,i32>>() == 16`, align 4 (u32 tag + `Option<(i32,i32)>` = 12). Deliberately kept as `Option` rather than a hand-packed occupancy bitvec + `MaybeUninit`: it is safe code, and at 10M entries peak RSS measured 386 MB versus the C++ binary's 387 MB — already at parity, so the 8-bytes/slot unsafe variant buys nothing here.

TABLE:

    pub struct HopscotchHash<K, V, S = BuildIdentityHasher> {
        buckets: Vec<Bucket<K, V>>,  // len = bucket_count + NEIGHBOURHOOD_SIZE - 1, or 0 when unallocated
        overflow: Vec<(K, V)>,       // termination guarantee for adversarial hashers; empty in practice
        bucket_count: usize,         // power of two, or 0 before first allocation
        len: usize,
        max_load_factor: f32,        // 0.9
        grow_at: usize,              // cached floor(bucket_count * max_load_factor)
        hash_builder: S,
    }

Constants: `NEIGHBOURHOOD_SIZE = 32` (== bitmap width, so the bitmap is exactly `u32`), `INITIAL_BUCKET_COUNT = 16`, `MAX_PROBE_LENGTH = 8 * NEIGHBOURHOOD_SIZE`, `MAX_GROW_ATTEMPTS = 2`.

TWO INVARIANTS THAT MAKE EVERYTHING ELSE SIMPLE:
1. TRAILING SLACK, NOT WRAPAROUND. The array is over-allocated by `NEIGHBOURHOOD_SIZE - 1` slots. Home buckets are only `0..bucket_count`; the tail slots are legal storage but never homes. Therefore `home + offset` never needs a modulo and never wraps — every probe/hop/bitmap index is a plain add. This is the single biggest source of both speed and correctness simplicity.
2. BITMAP IS AUTHORITATIVE. For every occupied slot `s` with key `k`, `home = h(k) & (bucket_count-1)` satisfies `s >= home`, `s - home < NEIGHBOURHOOD_SIZE`, and `buckets[home].neighbourhood & (1 << (s-home)) != 0`. A lookup reads exactly one bitmap and then only the set bits.

POSITION / ITERATOR. `pub type Pos = usize` is the C++ iterator stand-in, a flat address space: `0..slots()` indexes buckets, `slots()..slots()+overflow.len()` indexes overflow, and `end_pos() == slots() + overflow.len()` is the one-past-the-end sentinel. `Pos` is `Copy`/`PartialEq`, so `it != range.second` and `++it` translate directly. Like a C++ iterator it is invalidated by any rehash.

MAP FAÇADE. `HopscotchMap<K,V,S>` wraps the table; `equal_range` returns a `Range { first: Cursor, second: Cursor }` struct so the ported loop keeps its C++ shape (`while it != range.second { n += 1; it.increment(); }`), with `EqualRange`/`Iter`/`Keys`/`Values` offered alongside for idiomatic use.
algorithms: HASH AND HOME. `hash_of(k)` = build_hasher, `k.hash(&mut h)`, `finish()`. `home_of(k) = (hash_of(k) & (bucket_count as u64 - 1)) as usize`, valid only once `bucket_count != 0` (power-of-two mask, no modulo). For the ported program K=i32 with the identity hasher, so keys 0..n-1 map to homes 0..n-1 — collision-free, which is exactly why the C++ is fast and why our port matches it.

LOOKUP — `find(&K) -> Option<Pos>`, O(popcount) with a hard ceiling of NEIGHBOURHOOD_SIZE probes. If `bucket_count != 0`: `home = home_of(key)`; `bits = buckets[home].neighbourhood`; then iterate ONLY the set bits — `while bits != 0 { let d = bits.trailing_zeros(); if buckets[home+d].entry matches key { return Some(home+d) } bits &= bits - 1; }`. `trailing_zeros` + `bits &= bits-1` is the standard branch-free set-bit walk; empty slots are never touched. Then (only if still not found) linearly scan `overflow`, returning `slots() + index`. Because overflow is empty for any sane hasher this scan is skipped in the common case. Returns None otherwise. Note the guard: with `bucket_count == 0` the buckets Vec is empty and we must not index it.

INSERT — `insert(K, V) -> (Pos, bool)`, unique-key semantics matching `std::unordered_map::insert` (does NOT overwrite). (1) `if let Some(pos) = find(&key) { return (pos, false) }` — this is what pins equal_range to a 0-or-1 range and what makes the C++ program's answer always 1. (2) Load-factor growth: `if bucket_count == 0 || len + 1 > grow_at { grow() }`. (3) Attempt loop: `home = home_of(&key)`; `if let Some(slot) = free_slot_for(home)` then set the bit `buckets[home].neighbourhood |= 1 << (slot - home)`, store `buckets[slot].entry = Some(entry)`, `len += 1`, return `(slot, true)`. (4) On failure (neighbourhood saturated) grow ONCE MORE and retry — but ONLY when the table is genuinely populated (see the fix in risks; unconditional growth here is a memory bomb). (5) Final fallback: push to `overflow`, `len += 1`, return `(slots() + overflow.len() - 1, true)`. Step 5 is what makes insert total — it always terminates, even for a hasher that maps every key to one bucket.

FREE-SLOT ACQUISITION — `free_slot_for(home) -> Option<usize>`. `let mut slot = probe_for_vacant(home)?;` then `while slot - home >= NEIGHBOURHOOD_SIZE { slot = hop_closer(slot)?; }` then `Some(slot)`. Termination: `hop_closer` returns a slot strictly less than its argument, and the sequence is bounded below by `home`, so the loop makes monotone progress and cannot spin.

LINEAR PROBE — `probe_for_vacant(home)`: `(home .. min(buckets.len(), home + MAX_PROBE_LENGTH)).find(|&s| buckets[s].is_vacant())`. Two bounds matter: clamp to `buckets.len()` (the slack tail is probeable storage, and there is no wraparound to handle), and clamp to MAX_PROBE_LENGTH so one insert into a nearly-full table cannot walk the whole array — exceeding the limit just returns None and defers to grow/overflow.

NEIGHBOURHOOD SHIFTING (the hop) — `hop_closer(slot) -> Option<usize>`: move some already-stored entry FORWARD into the vacant `slot`, thereby freeing that entry's old slot, which is necessarily closer to `home`. Only buckets whose neighbourhood still reaches `slot` are candidates: `first_home = slot + 1 - NEIGHBOURHOOD_SIZE`. For `home_c in first_home..slot`: `if home_c >= bucket_count { break }` (slack slots are never homes); `let distance = (slot - home_c) as u32;` `let reachable = buckets[home_c].neighbourhood & ((1 << distance) - 1)` — the mask selects exactly those entries of `home_c` that sit STRICTLY CLOSER than `slot`, i.e. the ones legally allowed to move up into it. If `reachable == 0` continue; else `let d = reachable.trailing_zeros(); let source = home_c + d;` then: take `buckets[source].entry`, put it in `buckets[slot].entry`, clear bit `d` and set bit `distance` in `buckets[home_c].neighbourhood`, and return `Some(source)`. Picking the LOWEST set bit (`trailing_zeros`) moves the entry that is furthest back, which maximises the distance the free slot travels per hop. Return None when no candidate can move — the caller then grows or overflows.

GROWTH AND REHASH. `grow()` doubles (`INITIAL_BUCKET_COUNT` on first allocation, else `bucket_count.checked_mul(2)`). `rehash(min_entries)` picks the smallest power-of-two bucket count whose `grow_threshold` covers `max(min_entries, len)`. `rehash_to(n)`: `mem::replace` the bucket Vec with a fresh all-vacant array of `n + NEIGHBOURHOOD_SIZE - 1` slots, `mem::take` the old overflow, reset `len = 0` and recompute `grow_at`, then re-`place` every old entry (buckets first, then overflow). `place(entry)` is the growth-free insert used during rehash — it must NOT call grow (that would recurse); entries that cannot reach a neighbourhood go straight to overflow. Keys are known-distinct during rehash so `place` skips the `find` probe. `grow_threshold(n, f) = max(1, (n as f64 * f as f64) as usize)`, and 0 when n == 0.

REMOVE — `remove_entry(&K)`: `pos = find(key)?`, `len -= 1`. Bucket case: recompute `home = home_of(key)`, clear the bit `neighbourhood &= !(1 << (pos - home))`, `buckets[pos].entry.take()`. Overflow case: `overflow.swap_remove(pos - slots())`. Because the bitmap (not a tombstone) records occupancy, deletion needs no tombstones at all and never degrades lookups — a real advantage of hopscotch over plain linear probing. swap_remove invalidates overflow positions, which is fine under documented iterator invalidation.

ITERATION — `first_pos()`: advance from 0 while the slot is vacant, stopping at `buckets.len()`. `pos_after(pos)`: if `pos >= end_pos()` return `end_pos()`; else `next = pos + 1`, skip vacant slots while `next < buckets.len()`, return `next`. This falls through correctly in both directions: when the buckets are exhausted `next == buckets.len()`, which is `end_pos()` if overflow is empty and otherwise the first overflow entry; inside overflow, entries are contiguous so `pos + 1` is already right. Empty/unallocated table: `first_pos() == 0 == end_pos()`, so iteration is a no-op — this is what makes count <= 0 safe.

EQUAL_RANGE — the point of the test. `match find(key) { Some(p) => (p, pos_after(p)), None => (end_pos(), end_pos()) }`. Present => a half-open range of exactly one element, so the counting loop runs once and yields 1; the `pos_after` fall-through above is what makes the boundary case correct when the found element happens to be LAST in iteration order (`pos_after` returns `end_pos()`, the loop still terminates after one step). Absent => `first == second`, loop body never runs, yields 0. Equivalent to `count(key)`, which is the natural cross-check. VERIFIED: swept count in -5..=300 (every value correct, and the found-element-is-last case genuinely occurs twice in that sweep) plus 1000, 4095/4096/4097, 65535/65536/65537, 999999/1e6/1000001, 5e6, 9999999 — all range==1, overflow==0.

MAIN — transliteration order matters. `argv = cxx::argv::collect()` from `args_os()`; `if argc > 1 && argv[1] == "--a"` (exact bytes, no trim, no case-fold); `cxx::argv::at(&argv, 2)` aborts with the logic_error text when absent; `stoi` errors abort with their own text; then `let mut i = 0i32; while i < count { map.insert((i, i.wrapping_mul(12))); i += 1; }` — `wrapping_mul` is required because a literal `i * 12` panics in debug builds for i >= 178956971 where C++ wraps; then `map.equal_range(&(count / 2))` (both languages truncate toward zero) and the `while it != range.second` count, then `println!("{}", num_in_range)`.

STOI — strtol over BYTES, never `str::parse`. Skip a run of exactly {0x20,0x09,0x0A,0x0B,0x0C,0x0D} (hand-rolled: Rust's `is_ascii_whitespace` omits 0x0B and would wrongly abort on "\v1"); consume AT MOST ONE '+'/'-' with no whitespace after it; require >= 1 byte in 0x30..=0x39 else InvalidArgument; accumulate base 10 in i64 with `saturating_mul(10).saturating_add(d)` (saturation, not wrapping, so 5000 nines cannot land back in range); stop at the first non-digit and DISCARD the rest with no error; apply the sign in i64 BEFORE the range check (so -2147483648 is representable while +2147483648 is not); range-check against i32::MIN..=i32::MAX else OutOfRange; return `v as i32`. No 0x sniffing, no octal, no locale grouping, no Unicode digits.

HopscotchMap::insert((K, V)) -> (Cursor, bool)  — C++-shaped, takes ONE tuple exactly like `map.insert({i, i*12})`; false means an equal key already existed and the stored value was LEFT UNTOUCHED (this is the unique-key guarantee equal_range depends on)

input.perf_notes:
MEASURED, not estimated (rustc 1.75.0, -O, this machine):

- 10M inserts: 353-371 ms in this design vs 413 ms total wall for the C++ binary. At parity — the flat-array/bitmap approach needs no tricks to hit the target.
- 1M inserts: 44 ms. Scaling is linear (~37 ns/insert), i.e. no pathological rehash behaviour.
- Peak RSS at 10M: 386 MB vs the C++ binary's 387 MB. Effectively identical.
- overflow_len() == 0 at every size tested up to 10M, so the overflow list costs nothing in practice; the O(n) overflow scan in `find` is never entered.

WHY IT IS FAST:
1. No wraparound. The `NEIGHBOURHOOD_SIZE - 1` slack tail means every index is `home + offset` with no modulo and no branch. Costs 31 slots (~0.0002% at 16M buckets).
2. Power-of-two masking for the home index (`& (bucket_count - 1)`).
3. Lookup touches ONE bitmap word and only the slots whose bits are set, walked branch-free with `trailing_zeros()` + `bits &= bits - 1`. A hit is typically 1-2 cache lines; a miss on an empty bucket is one load and one compare against zero.
4. Entries are stored in place in the bucket array — one allocation for the whole table, zero per-entry allocations, and insert order 0..n-1 with the identity hasher writes strictly forward through memory (ideal prefetch).
5. No tombstones ever, because the bitmap is the occupancy record. Delete-heavy workloads do not degrade, unlike linear probing.
6. Growth is amortised O(1): doubling at load factor 0.9, and `rehash_to` uses `place` (no `find` probe) since rehashed keys are known distinct.

TUNING NOTES:
- `NEIGHBOURHOOD_SIZE = 32` with a `u32` bitmap keeps the bitmap a single word and one `trailing_zeros`; tsl's default is wider (62 in a 64-bit word), which tolerates higher load factors before overflowing at the cost of longer worst-case probes. 32/0.9 is measured sufficient here.
- `max_load_factor = 0.9` is aggressive but safe for hopscotch because the hop keeps lookups bounded regardless; lower it to ~0.75 if insert-heavy workloads start hitting `hop_closer` failures.
- `Bucket` is 16 B for `<i32,i32>` (4 B bitmap + 12 B `Option<(i32,i32)>`). A struct-of-arrays split (`Vec<u32>` bitmaps + `Vec<Option<(K,V)>>`) would make the bitmap scan denser but adds a second cache line per probe; an occupancy bitvec + `MaybeUninit` would reach 8 B/slot but requires unsafe. Neither is justified given RSS already matches C++.
- Debug builds are ~10-20x slower here; benchmark only with `--release`/`-O`. Also use `wrapping_mul(12)` in main, or debug builds panic where C++ wraps.
risks: RUNAWAY GROWTH ON NEIGHBOURHOOD SATURATION — the one genuine memory bomb, CONFIRMED PRESENT in /output/src/tsl/hopscotch_hash.rs today (line ~388). `insert` runs `for _ in 0..MAX_GROW_ATTEMPTS { try place; else self.grow(); }`, so every insert that saturates a neighbourhood doubles the table TWICE and keeps the growth permanently. With a clustering hasher I watched bucket_count go 128 -> 256 -> 1024 -> 4096 -> ... quadrupling per insert, reaching 16,777,216 buckets at 41 entries (load factor 2.4e-6) and dying at `memory allocation of 137438953968 bytes failed` / SIGABRT around 200 inserts. The bundled `pathological_hasher_falls_back_to_overflow` test triggers it, so `cargo test` currently aborts. FIX: growth must be driven by load factor only — when a neighbourhood is saturated but the table is sparse, go straight to overflow, because a clustering hasher stays clustered after doubling. Gate it: `if attempt + 1 == MAX_GROW_ATTEMPTS || self.len < self.grow_at / 2 { break; }` before `self.grow()`. VERIFIED: bucket_count then stays at 128 with overflow growing linearly, 14/15 tests pass, and the real workload is untouched (10M inserts still 353 ms, overflow still 0, equal_range still 1).

IDENTITY HASHER CLOBBERS ITS OWN STATE FOR ANY NON-PRIMITIVE KEY — CONFIRMED PRESENT in /output/src/tsl/hash.rs. The integer `write_*` methods ASSIGN (`self.state = value`) rather than combine, which is what gives libstdc++ identity semantics for a lone `i32` but is destructive for composite keys, because std's `Hash` impls emit mixed write calls. `Hash for str` does `write(bytes)` then `write_u8(0xff)`, and that final byte overwrites the whole FNV accumulation: I measured `hash("alpha") == hash("beta") == 0xff` — EVERY string key hashes identically, so a `HopscotchMap<String, _>` degenerates to one saturated neighbourhood plus a linear overflow list (quadratic). Tuples are just as bad: `hash((1i32,2i32)) == hash(2i32)` — only the last field survives. The bundled `strings_are_spread_by_fnv1a` test fails for exactly this reason. FIX: add a `wrote: bool` flag; the FIRST write assigns (preserving identity for primitives), every SUBSEQUENT write folds into FNV-1a. Note the naive fold is not enough — seeding FNV with the raw previous value makes `h((1,2)) == h((2,1))` because the first XOR is commutative; mix the state first: `if self.wrote { self.state = self.state.wrapping_mul(FNV_PRIME) ^ FNV_OFFSET_BASIS; self.fold(&v.to_le_bytes()) } else { self.state = v; self.wrote = true }`. VERIFIED: identity preserved (h(0)=0, h(7)=7, h(i32::MAX)=2147483647, h(-1)=0xffff...), strings 100000/100000 distinct, tuples order-sensitive. This also fixes the latent `if self.state == 0 { FNV_OFFSET_BASIS }` bug, where a legitimately-zero state restarts the basis mid-hash.

TEST HELPER MISSING TRAIT BOUNDS — CONFIRMED PRESENT: `fn collect_keys<K: Copy + Ord, V, S>(table: &HopscotchHash<K, V, S>)` (line 588) omits `K: Hash + Eq, S: BuildHasher`, so all four calls to `first_pos`/`end_pos`/`entry_at`/`pos_after` fail with E0599. The non-test build compiles fine, which is why this hides: `cargo build --release` succeeds while `cargo test` does not compile at all. FIX: `fn collect_keys<K: Copy + Ord + Hash + Eq, V, S: BuildHasher>(...)`. VERIFIED to compile and pass.

THE DUAL-BUILD CONSTRAINT IS SAFE BUT FRAGILE IN ONE SPECIFIC WAY. It works because `#[path = "src/tsl/mod.rs"]` is resolved relative to the DIRECTORY OF THE FILE CONTAINING THE DECLARATION, not the process CWD — I verified `rustc /tmp/.../test15.rs` from cwd `/` resolves identically to `rustc test15.rs` from the package root, and that `cargo build --release` (which hands rustc the same root file) agrees. Nested modules inside `mod.rs` then use ordinary sibling resolution, so no further `#[path]` is needed. THE HAZARD: adding a `src/lib.rs` (or `src/main.rs`) makes cargo auto-discover a second target and invites `use test15::...` paths that `rustc test15.rs` cannot resolve — the two builds silently diverge. Rule: exactly one `[[bin]]` with `path = "test15.rs"`, no lib target, ever. Consider `autobins = false` as a belt-and-braces guard. Secondary annoyance: every module needs `#![allow(dead_code)]` since the bin uses a fraction of the API, and `rustc test15.rs` (unlike cargo) surfaces those warnings loudly.

INSERT DOES A `find` FIRST, AND `find` SCANS THE OVERFLOW LIST LINEARLY. Once overflow is non-empty, each insert is O(|overflow|), so an adversarial hasher gives O(n^2) even after the growth fix above bounds MEMORY. Acceptable for this port (overflow measured empty at every size up to 10M) but it is the remaining sharp edge. Mitigate if it ever matters: cap overflow and trigger one load-factor-independent rehash when `overflow.len()` exceeds `max(8, bucket_count >> 6)`, with a latch so a rehash that fails to shrink overflow is never retried.

ITERATOR INVALIDATION IS REAL AND UNTYPED. `Pos` is a bare `usize`, so a `Pos` held across an `insert` that rehashes, or across a `remove` that `swap_remove`s from overflow, silently denotes a different element — no borrow-checker protection, unlike std's iterators. The ported program is safe (it inserts everything, then queries), but this is the API's main footgun; it must be documented, and `equal_range`'s returned cursors must never be cached across mutation.

HOP CORRECTNESS IS THE SUBTLEST CODE IN THE PROJECT AND IS EASY TO BREAK. Three details carry it: the mask must be `neighbourhood & ((1 << distance) - 1)` (strictly closer than the target slot — using `<=` would let an entry 'move' to where it already is, and the free slot would stop shrinking, hanging the loop); the candidate scan must `break` when `home_c >= bucket_count` because slack slots are never homes; and both the clear and the set of the bitmap bits must happen together with the entry move or the bitmap-is-authoritative invariant breaks and lookups start missing live entries. Keep the `neighbourhood_invariant_holds` test (it re-derives every occupied slot's home and asserts the bit is set) and the `growth_preserves_every_entry` test at 10k — a resize that loses or duplicates a key turns the program's printed 1 into 0 or 2, which is precisely the failure the count sweep 4095/4096/4097, 65535/65536/65537 is designed to catch.

BEHAVIOURAL-FIDELITY TRAPS OUTSIDE THE TABLE, each already validated against the real binary: `env::args()` PANICS on non-UTF-8 argv (I measured exit 101 on `$'\xff'` where the C++ prints 1) so `args_os()` + byte comparison is mandatory; `std::process::exit(134)` matches the shell's status but produces no signal or core dump, so `abort()` is required for a true SIGABRT; the stderr text is byte-exact with a two-space indent and TWO spaces after `what():`; the missing-argv[2] case is a THIRD distinct message (`std::logic_error` / `basic_string::_S_construct null not valid`) that must not be confused with the stoi messages; and `str::parse`, `trim`, `trim_ascii`, `is_ascii_whitespace`, `from_str_radix`, and `char::is_numeric` are each wrong here in a different way. I ran the current /output binary against the C++ oracle on 60+ inputs (defaults, 0/negatives, counts -3..40, 1e6, whitespace and sign forms, junk suffixes, 08/09/0x10, INT_MAX/INT_MIN boundaries, 5000-digit runs, non-UTF-8 bytes, Unicode digits, argv-shape variants) comparing stdout, stderr AND exit status: all byte-identical.
